newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: "Che Guevara's bones" on way to definitive test.
newsitem.headline: "Che Guevara's bones" on way to definitive test.

text.p: Remains believed to be those of Cuban guerrilla Ernesto "Che" Guevara were to arrive on Sunday in the Bolivian city of Santa Cruz for definitive identification.

Transportation by truck of the bones found last week in a mass grave near the southeastern Bolivian village of Vallegrande is the first step in their planned repatriation to Cuba. The same team of Cuban and Argentine scientists that found the bones will conduct scientific tests in Santa Cruz's Japanese Hospital to confirm the remains are Guevara's.

"The Bolivian government, in accordance with international agreements and requests by relatives, has decided to transport the remains ... for their definitive identification," Bolivian Interior Minister Victor Hugo Canelas told a midnight news conference in Vallegrande.

Scientific team leader Dr. Jorge Gonzalez told reporters earlier he had "the personal conviction" that one of seven skeletons found in the grave was Guevara's. The skeleton has a skull matching his heavy facial features and its hands are missing, he said.
The Bolivian troops who executed the communist icon in October 1967 cut off his hands so his fingerprints would serve as proof they had killed him. Then they buried the body in a secret location.

Gonzalez said final identification of the remains would require several days of tests. Scientists think the other six skeletons are those of Guevara's hapless band of Cuban, Bolivian and Peruvian rebels.

The Argentine-born doctor and hero of Cuba's 1959 revolution was trying to export communism to South America's mainland when he was captured, wounded and starving, on Oct. 8, 1967, and shot by a soldier in Vallegrande's school.

Bolivia began the quest for Guevara's bones in December 1995 after retired Gen. Mario Vargas Salinas broke two decades of military silence to say he could identify the spot where he ordered the burial of the guerrillas.
But he failed to locate the spot and the search has since been repeatedly suspended and resumed, with excavations centering on an airstrip outside Vallegrande, 480 miles (775 km) southeast of La Paz.
The search was relaunched in May based on new evidence, including the statement of a truck driver who said he had transported the bodies of Guevara and his comrades.

Impoverished Vallegrande has already declared Guevara's bones "the patrimony of the region" and wants to develop a local tourist industry around them. But Bolivia's government plans to give them to Guevara's family.
His Cuban wife, Aleida March, has requested that they be sent back to the Caribbean island for final burial.
